project.project_type: plan change / tenant improvement, mid-construction-document phase
project.description: Tenant improvement across two floors (97,910 SF total: Phase I West 56,966 SF, Phase II East 40,944 SF) changing Use Group from Business to Assembly (A-3, place of worship), with a specialty coffee cafe, playland/kids area, baptistries, and access-controlled door system. Main worship auditorium is programmed for 1,462 seats; the Next Gen (youth) auditorium for 260; the Adult Discipleship classroom (also used as an overflow chapel) for 435. This pass consolidates the September 8-9, 2026 site-visit summary with the fuller project document history from January through August 2026 (design reviews, coordination meetings, and the space program) pulled from the UNITE_PROJECTS/251006_TrinityChurch_ScottsdaleAZ shared drive folder. Two files in that folder -- 'Trinity Meeting Summary - 2026-05-12.docx' and its '(v2)' -- could not be opened (return empty content both via this tool and directly by the requester) and are excluded from this research; if their content is later recovered, re-run this pass to check for anything new.
project.excluded_documents_note: Most of the earlier (January-May 2026) meeting notes concern pure design/layout decisions with no code dimension (adult classroom count, bookstore security method, glass wall placement, green room privacy layout, specialty lighting themes, etc.) and were deliberately left out of the findings below -- they were reviewed but are not code-relevant. Only genuinely new code questions, and facts that sharpen an existing finding (like the confirmed occupant-load numbers), are reflected.

jurisdiction.notes: Confirmed from project specification title page: 10001 North 92nd Street, Scottsdale, AZ 85258. Zoning/parking is governed separately from the building code, at Scottsdale Revised Code Appendix B (Basic Zoning Ordinance), Article IX -- see library overview for the full adopted-code table, now including this distinction.

findings.question: Can a hand sanitizer station legally replace the hand wash sink at the specialty coffee cafe counter, which was ruled cost-prohibitive?
findings.source_quote: Cafe concept: Specialty coffee/cafe (not just drip coffee). Must comply with Maricopa County Health Department requirements for commercial food service. Hand wash sink at cafe was ruled cost-prohibitive -- replace with hand sanitizer station.

applicable_codes.code_body: Maricopa County Environmental Health Code, Ch. VIII Sec. 2
applicable_codes.edition_or_effective_date: current, references FDA Food Code 2017 Ed., effective 10/6/2021
applicable_codes.link_note: PDF loads directly from maricopa.gov; title/subject metadata confirms Maricopa County Environmental Health Code.

applicable_codes.code_body: FDA Food Code, 2017 Edition (official landing page)
applicable_codes.adopted_by: Maricopa County, by reference (no future editions adopted)
applicable_codes.link_note: This is the correct official FDA page, but fda.gov returns 401 to automated fetch -- could not confirm content just now. The verbatim section text was actually confirmed against a county-hosted mirror of the same document, see next entry.

applicable_codes.code_body: FDA Food Code, 2017 Edition (verified mirror, verbatim text confirmed)
applicable_codes.adopted_by: Maricopa County, by reference (no future editions adopted)
applicable_codes.link_note: A county health department's mirror of the same FDA Food Code text; this is the copy the exact section wording was actually read from during research, since fda.gov itself blocked automated access.

findings.rule_in_plain_language: A dedicated handwashing sink is required at any food/beverage prep or service bar; a specialty espresso/steamed-milk counter is a TCS (time/temperature control for safety) food operation and falls under MCESD's 'Open Food Service and Beverage Establishment' category, which requires a hand sink centrally located and directly accessible from all bars. Hand sanitizer is only ever a supplement applied after washing at a sink (2-301.16(A)(3)), never a substitute. The only sink-substitution exception (chemically treated towelettes, not sanitizer, under 5-203.11(C)) is limited to mobile/temporary establishments and vending locations, which this permanent counter is not.

problem_identified.description: High probability of plan-review rejection at Maricopa County Environmental Services. This is not a gray area under the adopted code.

proposed_solutions.option: Compact plumbed ADA hand sink (9x9 to 15 inch wall-mount or corner unit) tucked at the end of the counter run
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Smallest true footprint, fully code-compliant, one-time plumbing tie-in cost.

proposed_solutions.option: Point-of-use tankless/instant electric water heater dedicated to that one sink
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Avoids extending the main building water heater loop to a satellite counter; adds a small electric water heater cost but usually cheaper than a long hot water run.

proposed_solutions.option: Reconfigure counter layout (move pastry case/POS) to free 12-18 inches of run for the sink
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Often cheaper than moving walls; may require re-coordinating other cafe millwork already in progress.

proposed_solutions.option: Self-contained portable hand-wash cart
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: MCESD recognizes these mainly for catering/mobile use; likely accepted only as a stop-gap with prior written approval, not as a final permitted installation -- higher inspector scrutiny and daily fill/drain labor. Not recommended as the end-state fix.

findings.verification_note: Call MCESD Plan Review (602-506-6824) to confirm the establishment classification in writing and finalize the cafe layout before the menu/plan submission. An architect should confirm final sink placement against ADA clearance and the 25-foot accessibility rule from all bars.

findings.question: Can the site-visit plan changes (playland reconfiguration, egress/security door changes, restroom stall increase, baptistry plumbing, MEP changes) be implemented as field revisions after permit issuance, without a formal resubmission to the City of Scottsdale?
findings.source_quote: Do NOT resubmit plans to the city with all current changes. Proceed with the permit using existing drawings... All plan changes discussed at the site visit will be incorporated as field revisions after the permit is issued (not as a resubmission). This avoids triggering a full re-review by the city.

applicable_codes.adopted_by: City of Scottsdale, Ordinance No. 4550 / Resolution No. 12498, SRC Ch. 31 (this section is not locally amended, so the base model-code text applies as-is)
applicable_codes.link_note: Rendered directly with a real headless browser (ICC's site blocks simple HTTP fetches but not an actual browser) and read the live page. Confirmed: page is titled 'Excerpt From: 2021 International Building Code (IBC)' with no state attached (the true base model text), breadcrumb 2021 IBC / CHAPTER 1 / SECTION 107 / [A] 107.4, and the rendered section text reads verbatim: 'Work shall be installed in accordance with the approved construction documents, and any changes made during construction that are not in compliance with the approved construction documents shall be resubmitted for approval as an amended set of construction documents.' Matches what was already quoted in rule_in_plain_language exactly. Also separately confirmed, by reading Scottsdale's own amendment ordinance directly, that Scottsdale does not locally amend this section. Original citation had linked to up.codes/s/amended-construction-documents, which actually resolved to the 2024 Texas Windstorm Insurance Association Building Code; corrected.

findings.rule_in_plain_language: IBC Section 107.4: "Work shall be installed in accordance with the approved construction documents, and any changes made during construction that are not in compliance with the approved construction documents shall be resubmitted for approval as an amended set of construction documents." The Building Official's judgment on the scope/extent of the change governs since no numeric threshold is given. Egress door location/hardware, security/lockdown door hardware, converting classroom space to lobby/assembly space, new restroom stalls, and new baptistry plumbing and water heaters are all plan-reviewed life-safety or systems items under standard code administration -- not typically 'field revision' territory.

problem_identified.description: Real, non-trivial process risk. If Scottsdale's inspectors or plan reviewers determine the field changes exceed approved plans, likely outcomes include a stop-work order, a required retroactive amended-document submittal, re-inspection of completed work at the contractor's cost and delay, and a delayed certificate of occupancy given that C.O. issuance depends on egress and life-safety systems matching approved plans for the B-to-A conversion.

proposed_solutions.option: Proactively disclose the site-visit changes to the assigned plan reviewer now, even while pursuing permit issuance on the original drawings, and get their determination in writing
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Small time cost now; substantially reduces risk of a stop-work order or retroactive resubmittal later.

proposed_solutions.option: Selectively resubmit only the highest-risk items (egress door location/hardware, the security door, and anything affecting occupant load/occupancy classification such as the lobby/playland reconfiguration) as a formal plan revision
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Keeps the bulk of the permit moving on the original schedule while addressing the items most likely to trigger enforcement action.

proposed_solutions.option: Also route the restroom stall count increase and baptistry plumbing/water heater additions through at least a plumbing plan revision
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: These affect fixture-count code compliance and new mechanical/electrical loads; handling as true field revisions carries similar risk to the egress items.

proposed_solutions.option: Request a pre-application/pre-construction meeting with Scottsdale Building Safety given the compounded occupancy change
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Gets a Building-Official-level read on scope before construction rather than risking an inspector's field determination mid-project.

findings.verification_note: No Scottsdale-specific written field-revision definition was located despite thorough searching (the 107.4 code text itself is now directly browser-verified against ICC's own site, see applicable_codes above). Confirm directly with Scottsdale Building Safety / One Stop Shop (480-312-2500) or the assigned plan reviewer before proceeding on the current strategy.

findings.question: Is the project's parking strategy (a Traffic Impact Analysis plus shared-parking agreements with neighboring properties plus the adjacent garage) actually sufficient to satisfy Scottsdale's zoning parking requirement for each separately permitted phase?
findings.source_quote: During the pre-app, when we told the city we're going to break the tenant improvement plans into separate packages for separate permits, they said when we come in, we need to prove that we have ample parking for each piece... their functional need is one space for every two seats in worship... They've already got over 200 committed to the building just due south of them.

applicable_codes.code_body: Scottsdale Revised Code, Appendix B (Basic Zoning Ordinance), Article IX, Parking and Loading Requirements
applicable_codes.section: Table 9.103.A (parking ratio for churches/places of worship); Sec. 9.107 (Remote parking); Sec. 9.104.E/F (Shared Parking Program / Parking Master Plan)
applicable_codes.edition_or_effective_date: current, includes amendment by Ord. No. 4500 (Res. No. 12141), 5-18-2021
applicable_codes.link_note: Municode's own site is a JS application that blocks automated fetching; text was pulled from a cyclesafe.com PDF mirror and cross-checked against an elaws.us Scottsdale mirror, both showing consistent section numbering and the same amendment citation. Recommend the firm pull a certified copy via Municode or the City Clerk before this citation goes into a stamped submission.

findings.rule_in_plain_language: Table 9.103.A requires 1 parking space per 4 fixed seats in the main sanctuary (or 1 per 30 SF of sanctuary area with no fixed seating), plus 1 space per 300 SF of classroom/meeting area on top of that. At 1,462 auditorium seats, the sanctuary alone requires 366 spaces at code minimum -- the design team's internal '1 space per 2 seats' planning rule (about 731 spaces for the sanctuary) is roughly double the actual code minimum, so that internal rule is conservative, not a shortfall. Nothing in the zoning ordinance treats separately permitted 'East side' and 'West side' packages as legally separate sites for parking purposes -- Sec. 9.102.A ties the requirement to each permit as a triggering event, checked against the cumulative site requirement, unless a Parking Master Plan (Sec. 9.104.F) is filed to formally demonstrate adequacy per phase. Off-site/shared spaces (the neighbor's ~200+ committed spaces, and any additional agreements) only count toward the requirement if they go through Sec. 9.107 (Remote parking) or Sec. 9.104.E/F: this requires a written agreement approved by both the Zoning Administrator and the City Attorney, recorded against both properties at the Maricopa County Recorder's Office, with a minimum 5-year term, and the remote lot must be within 600 feet of the served property via a safe, continuous pedestrian route. The adjacent parking garage counts like ordinary on-site parking if it is on the same legal lot; if it is on a separate lot, it needs the same Sec. 9.107 treatment as any other off-site lot.

problem_identified.description: Not a design or code-compliance problem -- the strategy itself (TIA plus shared parking plus garage) is a normal, code-recognized path the zoning ordinance has purpose-built tools for. The real risk is procedural and timing-related: a recorded, City Attorney-approved agreement is required before permit issuance for any off-site/shared spaces counted toward the requirement. 'In progress' conversations or a letter of intent with the neighboring property are not sufficient at the point a permit is sought. If the East/West permits are pursued as informally separate 'locations' without a filed Parking Master Plan, the city could also treat each package as needing to independently prove parking adequacy without crediting the other side's committed spaces.

proposed_solutions.option: Confirm the shared-parking neighbor's lot is within the 600-foot Sec. 9.107 distance limit via a safe pedestrian route, now, before relying on it in the parking calculation
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: If it fails the distance test, the project needs a different parking solution or a variance -- better to know before the TIA and permit submittal are finalized.

proposed_solutions.option: Get the Remote Parking Agreement (or Shared Parking / Parking Master Plan agreement) drafted, approved by the Zoning Administrator and City Attorney, and recorded with the Maricopa County Recorder well ahead of the West-side permit submission
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: This is a real lead-time item involving another property owner and two city approvals -- start it now rather than treating it as a formality that can catch up later.

proposed_solutions.option: File a formal Parking Master Plan (Sec. 9.104.F) covering both the East and West permit packages as phases of one plan
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Gives the city the phase-by-phase adequacy demonstration it is asking for, and avoids the East/West split being read as two independent parking obligations.

findings.verification_note: Confirm the exact current text of Table 9.103.A, Sec. 9.107, and Sec. 9.104.E/F against a certified Municode copy or directly with Scottsdale Planning & Development Services before finalizing the parking narrative in the TIA or permit submittal -- Municode's own site could not be automated-fetch-verified in this research pass.

findings.question: Is providing only attachment/connection details (not full structural calculations) for the suspended AVL rigging, LED walls, and speaker clusters over the main auditorium sufficient for Scottsdale plan review?
findings.source_quote: Structural/rigging documentation expectations: GC/engineer will provide needed structural steel; Amplio provides rigging details from structure to equipment. However, Jerry flagged that Scottsdale jurisdictions may require structural calcs and more complete documentation (not just details), similar to other recent projects; Amplio confirmed this is doable and offered to share a sample.

applicable_codes.adopted_by: City of Scottsdale (Chapter 16 amendment only touches flood-hazard-area Sec. 1612.3; Sec. 1613 seismic design is not locally amended)
applicable_codes.section: Sec. 1613.1 (nonstructural components must be designed per ASCE 7 Chapter 13); Table 1604.5 (Risk Category III at occupant load 300+ in one area); Ch. 17, Sec. 1705.13 (special inspections for designated seismic systems/MEP component anchorage); Sec. 107.3.4 and 107.3.4.1 (deferred submittals)
applicable_codes.link_note: ICC's page for this chapter is a JS-rendered SPA that could not be scraped directly in this pass (unlike Sec. 107.4 and Sec. 1010.1.2, which were separately browser-verified). Section numbers and requirements were corroborated across structuremag.org's 2021 IBC significant-changes coverage and a Utah state facilities-management nonstructural-components guidance document, and independently against a South Carolina municipality's own 'Statement of Special Inspections, 2021 IBC Chapter 17' form reproducing the identical model-code section numbers. Scottsdale's own amendment ordinance was read directly and confirmed not to touch Sec. 1613 or Chapter 17 at all.

findings.rule_in_plain_language: Rigging, LED walls, speaker clusters, and truss permanently attached to the roof/ceiling structure are "nonstructural components" that must be designed to resist seismic effects under ASCE 7 Chapter 13, not just detailed for gravity/attachment hardware. The main auditorium (1,462 occupants) is Risk Category III under IBC Table 1604.5 (more than 300 people in one area), which raises the required Component Importance Factor and can trigger a manufacturer-certification or special-inspection requirement for the anchorage under IBC Chapter 17. A generic beam-clamp catalog cut sheet does not, by itself, satisfy this -- the code calls for an actual engineered design of the specific installed loads and attachment points, which in practice means calculations sealed by a licensed engineer. The correct path is a deferred submittal under IBC Sec. 107.3.4/107.3.4.1: the engineer of record flags the rigging/AVL package as deferred on the approved drawings, the specialty contractor's engineer submits sealed calculations, the EOR reviews them for general conformance, and the building official approves before installation.

problem_identified.description: Real risk of rejection or correction cycles at Scottsdale plan review if the AVL contractor's sample package is only attachment/connection details without sealed calculations. This appears to be the base 2021 IBC being enforced as written (Scottsdale's own ordinance does not add anything extra here), not a Scottsdale-specific overlay -- so it should be planned for as a standard requirement, not treated as unusual local strictness.

proposed_solutions.option: Have the AVL contractor's engineer prepare a proper delegated-design package: sealed calculations addressing gravity, seismic (ASCE 7 Ch. 13, correct Component Importance Factor for Risk Category III), and any other governing loads for the actual as-installed truss, LED wall, and speaker cluster weights at their specific attachment points
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: This is the compliant path and is what the contractor already offered to provide as a 'sample package' -- confirm it actually includes sealed calculations, not just hardware details, before treating the submittal as complete.

proposed_solutions.option: Have the engineer of record formally list the rigging/AVL attachment scope as a deferred submittal on the approved construction documents per IBC 107.3.4.1, and route the delegated engineer's calculations through the EOR for a general-conformance review before submitting to the building official
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Keeps the process on the record and avoids field installation happening before the deferred package is actually approved.

proposed_solutions.option: Confirm with the structural engineer of record whether the anchorage will require special inspection under IBC Chapter 17 given the project's Seismic Design Category, and schedule that inspection alongside the rest of the special-inspection program
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Avoids a late-discovered inspection requirement holding up rigging installation or final sign-off.

findings.verification_note: Confirm the project's actual Seismic Design Category and the resulting Component Importance Factor with the structural engineer of record, and confirm the exact special-inspection trigger with Scottsdale Building Safety, since these depend on site-specific seismic parameters not available from document review alone.

findings.question: Is it code-compliant to retain both a dedicated egress-only door and a separate lockable security door on the kids ministry classroom hallway, given the reduced number of secure doors?
findings.source_quote: Lockdown/security: both the new egress door AND the existing interior security door are to be retained. The egress door is life safety only; the security door is needed for midweek use when students and kids share the space.

applicable_codes.adopted_by: City of Scottsdale (Chapter 10 not locally amended)
applicable_codes.link_note: Original citation linked to up.codes/s/locking-arrangements-in-educational-occupancies, a bare aggregator URL that actually resolves to the 2021 Illinois Building Code, not Arizona/Scottsdale. Replaced with a neutral industry-commentary source, confirmed to load and discuss this exact section, that does not claim to be any specific jurisdiction's official page.

findings.rule_in_plain_language: A door may be locked to keep intruders out of a classroom/occupied room, provided: it can be unlocked from outside with a key or approved means; the interior egress hardware remains fully code-compliant (single-motion release, no key/tool/special knowledge, panic hardware required if occupant load is 50 or more); listed panic hardware, fire door hardware, and closers are not modified; and any fire-door alteration follows NFPA 80. Keeping a dedicated, hardware-clean egress-only door separate from the lockdown security door is a sound and commonly used strategy -- it avoids stacking a security lock and an access-control lock on the same door leaf, which is where most inspection failures happen.

problem_identified.description: The two-door approach is reasonable in principle, but three items are not resolved by document research alone and need the fire marshal's or plan reviewer's sign-off: (1) the final occupancy classification of the kids ministry space (Assembly incidental use vs. Group E vs. Group I-4 day care), which determines which locking section legally applies; (2) whether reducing the number of secure doors facing the hallway drops the room below the required number of exit access doorways or exceeds allowable common path of travel for the child occupant load (a separate egress-count question from the locking-hardware question); (3) confirmation that the security door, when locked during lockdown, is genuinely secondary to (not a substitute for) the dedicated egress door's compliance.

proposed_solutions.option: Confirm occupancy classification of the kids ministry space with the plan reviewer before finalizing the door count
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Resolves which code section applies and whether the 50-occupant panic-hardware threshold is triggered.

proposed_solutions.option: Have the architect verify exit access doorway count and common path of travel for the reconfigured space against IBC Table 1006.2.1 using the actual child occupant load
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Confirms the reduced secure-door count does not create an separate egress deficiency independent of the locking-hardware question.

findings.verification_note: Section numbering and requirements corroborated across multiple independent secondary sources (up.codes, idighardware.com), not read verbatim from ICC due to access blocks. Needs Scottsdale Fire Prevention/Building plan review sign-off on the specific room layout and occupant load.

findings.question: How much of this project's budget may be required for accessible path-of-travel upgrades given the scale of alteration and the occupancy change, and is this based on the alteration cost or the building's assessed value?
findings.source_quote: ADA compliance required throughout: ambulatory stalls, swing-out doors, 5-foot turning radius.

applicable_codes.code_body: Federal ADA / DOJ Title III regulation
applicable_codes.section: 28 CFR 36.403, Alterations: Path of travel; 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design Sec. 202.4
applicable_codes.link_note: Federal eCFR, read directly during research; no jurisdiction-mirroring risk since this is a single national source, not a multi-state aggregator.

applicable_codes.adopted_by: State of Arizona, A.R.S. Sec. 41-1492 et seq., Arizona Administrative Code Title 10 Ch. 3 Art. 4
applicable_codes.edition_or_effective_date: current, incorporates 2010 ADA Standards and 28 CFR 36.401-36.406 by reference
applicable_codes.link_note: URL is specifically an Arizona-titled page (not a generic aggregator slug), but returned 403 to re-verification just now. The Arizona Secretary of State's own PDF (apps.azsos.gov/public_services/Title_10/10-03.pdf) is the primary source and was also blocked from automated re-verification; confirm either in a normal browser before relying on this citation.

findings.rule_in_plain_language: This is commonly misunderstood as a percentage of the building's assessed value -- it is not. The rule is: when an alteration is made to a primary function area, the accessible path of travel from the site entrance through the altered area (plus the restrooms, drinking fountains, and phones serving it) must be brought up to current accessibility standards, up to a cost cap of 20 percent of the cost of that specific alteration. Beyond that cap the additional cost is considered disproportionate and is not required, but the 20 percent must still be spent, prioritized in this order: accessible entrance, then route to the altered area, then at least one accessible restroom, then phones/fountains.

problem_identified.description: For a project of this scale (97,910 SF, multi-phase, changing occupancy from Business to Assembly), the path-of-travel obligation is very likely to apply broadly and repeatedly -- each discrete phase of alteration triggers its own 20-percent-of-that-phase's-cost analysis for the route serving it. This is a budgeting and scoping issue more than a blocker, but it needs to be planned for rather than discovered during plan review.

proposed_solutions.option: Document existing accessible-route deficiencies now (parking to entrance, entrance to each altered area, existing restroom compliance) as a baseline before construction
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Establishes what must be fixed and gives a defensible record if the disproportionality cap is invoked later.

proposed_solutions.option: Budget a per-phase contingency line equal to up to 20 percent of that phase's construction cost for path-of-travel upgrades
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Avoids a late-stage budget surprise; may still be less than full compliance would cost if deficiencies are extensive.

findings.verification_note: Confirm the specific IEBC alteration-classification level (Level 1/2/3) that applies to each phase with the City of Scottsdale, since that affects which A117.1 edition and threshold calculations apply.

findings.question: Is it code-compliant for each toddler/preschool 'Jack and Jill' restroom (shared between two classrooms) to contain only a toilet, with the required handwashing lavatory instead located in the separate, adjoining classroom rather than in the restroom itself?
findings.source_quote: Separate Bathroom, toilet only. Dutch doors for restroom (both sides) with emergency/override release... Toddler toilet only in Jack and Jill restrooms. Separate toddler handwashing sink in classroom.

applicable_codes.adopted_by: City of Scottsdale, Resolution No. 12501, SRC Ch. 31 Art. IV (this section is not locally amended)
applicable_codes.link_note: ICC's own page returned 403 to automated fetch. Exact section number and verbatim text independently corroborated by an official Indiana Dept. of Homeland Security written code interpretation quoting the identical clause from the same numbered section, plus multiple jurisdictions (e.g. NYC Building Code) adopting the same IPC language verbatim at 405.3.2.

applicable_codes.code_body: Arizona Revised Statutes -- child-care licensing exemption
applicable_codes.link_note: Fetched directly from azleg.gov. Confirms a religious institution's nursery/kids-ministry program conducted with its services is exempt from state child-care-facility licensing, with no stated hours-per-week cap -- so Arizona Dept. of Health Services childcare plumbing rules (A.A.C. Title 9 Ch. 5) do not layer on top of the base IPC for a weekend-only program.

findings.rule_in_plain_language: IPC 405.3.2 requires the lavatory to be in the same room as the water closet it serves, but only for toilet rooms classified as 'public' or 'employee' use -- a 'private' toilet room (a single fixture, with restricted, non-walk-in access) is not covered by this same-room rule. An official Indiana interpretation of this identical IPC section approved a single-user children's toilet room, accessed from only one classroom, with the lavatory located in that classroom, on the reasoning that a single fixture with access limited to one classroom is not 'public.' Trinity's configuration differs in one respect that matters: each toilet room here is shared between two classrooms (a Jack-and-Jill arrangement), not one -- a closer call the code itself does not resolve with a bright line, since the IPC has no defined threshold for how many rooms keep a toilet room 'private.'

problem_identified.description: Genuinely ambiguous, leaning toward a real compliance risk given the two-classroom-shared factor -- an out-of-state persuasive interpretation supports the current design for a single-classroom case, but Trinity's two-classroom sharing is a materially different fact pattern the code doesn't clearly address. With roughly 15 of these restrooms across the kids ministry area, a rejected assumption at plan review would mean costly, repetitive rework.

proposed_solutions.option: Get a written interpretation from Scottsdale Building Safety plan review before proceeding, citing the Indiana precedent as support for treating each restroom as 'private' rather than 'public'
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: No added cost if approved; carries the risk and delay of an unfavorable determination discovered mid-design or at permit review.

proposed_solutions.option: Add one compact wall-hung lavatory inside each toilet room in addition to the classroom toddler sink
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Resolves the ambiguity outright regardless of how 'public' is interpreted, at modest added plumbing cost across roughly 15 rooms -- the safer, lower-risk fix given the volume of rooms at stake.

findings.verification_note: The Arizona child-care licensing exemption (A.R.S. 36-884(2)) is verified primary source and applies as long as the program stays tied to weekend religious services; it would need re-examination if the church later adds standalone weekday daycare hours. The IPC 405.3.2 'public vs. private' classification for a two-classroom-shared restroom is a genuine plan-reviewer judgment call, not a settled rule -- get it in writing before relying on it across all 15 rooms.

findings.question: Now that the main auditorium's actual seating capacity is programmed (1,462 seats), do the automatic sprinkler and fire alarm/voice-communication requirements for the converted Assembly occupancy apply, and at what level?
findings.source_quote: Auditorium Seating: 1,462 [capacity], 13,382 SF... Next Gen Auditorium: 260 people @ 25 SF per person... Adults Classroom [also functions as a chapel]: 435 person capacity.

applicable_codes.adopted_by: City of Scottsdale (Chapter 9 fire protection provisions not locally amended in a way that affects these thresholds)
applicable_codes.section: 903.2.1.3 (automatic sprinkler system, Group A-3); 907.2.1 (manual fire alarm, Group A); 907.5.2.2 (emergency voice/alarm communication system)
applicable_codes.link_note: Same JS-rendered-SPA limitation as the other ICC chapter-index pages; the underlying section numbers and thresholds (12,000 SF fire area or occupant load 300+ for sprinklers; 300+ for manual alarm; 1,000+ for voice/alarm communication) are long-standing IBC text confirmed across multiple independent state/municipal code portals reproducing the identical 2021 IBC provisions verbatim, and were not found to be touched by Scottsdale's own amendment ordinance.

findings.rule_in_plain_language: IBC 903.2.1.3 requires an automatic sprinkler system throughout a Group A-3 fire area where the fire area exceeds 12,000 SF, or the occupant load of the fire area is 300 or more, or the fire area is on a floor other than the level of exit discharge -- the main auditorium's 1,462-seat capacity clears the 300-occupant threshold by nearly 5x, on top of its 13,382 SF footprint also exceeding the 12,000 SF fire-area threshold independently. IBC 907.2.1 requires a manual fire alarm system in Group A occupancies at occupant load 300+; 907.5.2.2 requires a full emergency voice/alarm communication system (not just manual pull stations) once occupant load reaches 1,000 or more. At 1,462, the main auditorium clears both thresholds -- this is not a borderline call.

problem_identified.description: Not a design defect -- these are standard, unavoidable consequences of the Business-to-Assembly conversion at this scale, now confirmed with real numbers rather than an estimate. The Next Gen auditorium (260) and Adult Discipleship room (435, used as an overflow chapel) each need their own occupant-load check against these same thresholds for their respective fire areas, since 435 also clears 300 on its own. This is a budget and systems-design item that should already be assumed in scope, not something to discover as a surprise late in design.

proposed_solutions.option: Confirm the sprinkler and fire alarm/voice-communication scope already reflects all three assembly spaces (main auditorium 1,462, Adult Discipleship/chapel 435, Next Gen 260) at their correct individual occupant loads with the fire protection engineer
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Avoids a late-stage systems-design gap; the Adult Discipleship room's 435-person capacity independently triggers the same 300-occupant sprinkler/alarm thresholds as the main auditorium and should not be treated as a lower-tier space.

findings.verification_note: Section thresholds are well-established, unamended IBC text corroborated across many independent sources; recommend confirming the exact current wording against a licensed ICC/UpCodes source before it goes into a stamped fire-protection narrative.

findings.question: Do the roughly 90 doors receiving key card/fob access control readers need special egress hardware under the building code?
findings.source_quote: Approximately 90 doors total (77 interior) to receive power and data for key card / key fob access control readers.

applicable_codes.adopted_by: City of Scottsdale (Chapter 10 not locally amended)
applicable_codes.section: 1010.2.10, Access-Controlled Egress Doors (2021 numbering; renumbered again in later editions)
applicable_codes.link_note: Loads directly and discusses this exact section. Neutral industry commentary (Allegion/Lori Greene) rather than an official code page, chosen because ICC's own site blocks automated verification; it does not misrepresent itself as a specific state's adopted code.

findings.rule_in_plain_language: Where a card-reader/fob system controls the egress side of a door on a required means of egress, the code requires: a sensor that detects an approaching occupant and unlocks the door; a lock that fails safe (unlocks) on loss of power to the lock or sensor; and a manual push-button override mounted 40-48 inches above the floor, within 5 feet of the door, marked with signage, that keeps the door unlocked for at least 30 seconds when pressed. This only applies to doors where the reader affects the egress-side hardware -- if readers control entry only and the interior lever/panic hardware always operates freely, ordinary door hardware rules apply instead.

problem_identified.description: Not a blocker, but a door-by-door verification item across roughly 90 doors -- worth resolving with the hardware consultant before installation rather than after.

proposed_solutions.option: Have the electrical engineer/hardware consultant confirm, door by door, which locking topology is used (electrified mortise lock/strike with free-egress trim vs. true two-sided access control)
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Determines which subset of the 90 doors actually need the sensor/push-button/signage package -- avoids over-speccing hardware on doors that don't need it.

findings.verification_note: ICC's own code pages returned a 403 to automated fetch during research; section numbering and requirements were corroborated across multiple independent hardware-industry and code-consulting sources, not read verbatim from ICC. Confirm exact current text against a licensed ICC/UpCodes source, and note that section numbers shift between the 2018, 2021, and 2024 editions -- a common source of citation errors.

findings.question: Can a roll-up/overhead freight door at the Production/Receiving area serve as, or be located along, a required means of egress path, given that people may need to egress through or near this area?
findings.source_quote: Roll-up doors vs double doors may not be optimal operationally (ease of daily open/close, moving carts, worship egress conflicts)... remove roll-up at chair/table storage end if it conflicts with operations... keep roll-up only where it truly supports flexibility without creating egress issues.

applicable_codes.adopted_by: City of Scottsdale (Chapter 10 not locally amended)
applicable_codes.link_note: Rendered directly with a real headless browser and read the live ICC page, same technique used for Sec. 107.4. Confirmed verbatim text: 'Egress doors shall be of the side-hinged swinging door, pivoted door, or balanced door types,' followed by nine narrow exceptions (small private spaces with occupant load 10 or less, Group I-3 detention, critical/intensive care rooms, single-dwelling-unit doors, revolving doors, specific power-operated horizontal sliding assemblies, power-operated doors, R-1 sleeping-unit bathrooms, and manually operated horizontal sliding doors serving occupant load 10 or less). Overhead, coiling, and roll-up doors appear nowhere in the permitted types or the nine exceptions.

findings.rule_in_plain_language: A roll-up, coiling, or overhead door can never itself be the code-recognized 'egress door' -- no exception in Sec. 1010.1.2 covers it. It can still be installed for freight/cart movement as long as it is not the door relied upon to satisfy egress-door-type, egress-width, or exit-access requirements. A separate, properly sized swinging door provided in the same wall/area, sized for the actual occupant load and travel distance, is the standard and fully compliant way to have both a freight opening and a code-recognized egress path in the same location -- which is exactly the direction the design team is already leaning ('remove roll-up... where it conflicts,' 'keep roll-up only where it truly supports flexibility without creating egress issues').

problem_identified.description: Not a problem if executed as the design team is already planning: keep the roll-up for freight only and provide a separate dedicated swinging door for any egress function through this area. Worth confirming a few secondary triggers on that swinging door rather than leaving it as an open item.

proposed_solutions.option: Confirm whether the receiving area's occupant load reaches 50 (triggering swing-direction-of-travel under 1010.1.2.1) or whether the door serves a Group A fire area requiring panic hardware, and specify the swinging door's hardware accordingly
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: Ensures the 'compliant by default' solution doesn't miss a secondary hardware requirement once actual occupant load and adjacency are finalized.

proposed_solutions.option: If the receiving-area wall is a rated fire/smoke separation (e.g., separating S-occupancy storage from the A-occupancy worship space), confirm the swinging door gets a listed fire-rated assembly independent of its egress compliance, and that any roll-up door penetrating the same rated wall is itself a listed fire/smoke-rated rolling door assembly per NFPA 80
proposed_solutions.tradeoffs: These are two separate code questions (fire separation vs. egress) that both apply to the same wall if it happens to be rated -- confirm with the architect whether that wall is in fact a rated separation before assuming only the egress rule applies.

findings.verification_note: The egress-door-type rule itself is now directly browser-verified against ICC's own site. The occupant-load and fire-rating questions above are contingent on the final receiving-area layout and adjacency, which should be confirmed with the architect and fire protection engineer as the design finalizes.

findings.question: Do the expanding restroom doors (women's restroom to approximately 15 stalls, men's restroom expanded accordingly) need to swing in the direction of egress travel under the IBC 50-person occupant load threshold?
findings.source_quote: Confirm door swing direction per IBC 50-person occupancy threshold.

applicable_codes.adopted_by: City of Scottsdale (Chapter 10 not locally amended; section text unchanged from 2018 IBC)
applicable_codes.link_note: Original citation linked to up.codes/s/direction-of-swing, a bare aggregator URL that actually resolves to the 2021 Illinois Building Code, not Arizona/Scottsdale. Replaced with a neutral industry-commentary source, confirmed to load and quote this exact requirement, that does not claim to be any specific jurisdiction's official page.

findings.rule_in_plain_language: Side-hinged swinging doors, pivoted doors, and balanced doors must swing in the direction of egress travel where they serve a room or area with an occupant load of 50 or more, or a Group H occupancy. The threshold is based on the occupant load of the specific room or area the door serves, not automatically the occupant load of the larger assembly space it connects to. A 15-stall women's restroom and a similarly expanded men's restroom each have a room occupant load well under 50 even counting generously by fixture count, so on the plain text of this section the restroom doors themselves are not mandatorily required to swing in the direction of egress travel. The threshold clearly does apply to the main sanctuary/assembly space's own exit doors, which is a separate design question already understood to require sprinkler/occupant-load-appropriate egress design.

problem_identified.description: Likely not a blocker for the restroom doors specifically, based on the room-occupant-load reading of this section.

findings.verification_note: The room-vs-space occupant-load interpretation is professional consensus rather than a directly quotable definitional clause in the code. Recommend confirming this interpretation with the Scottsdale plans examiner in writing, since AHJ interpretation of 'area served' can vary, especially if the restroom vestibule/corridor lacks a separating door from the larger space.
